extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in philosophy of science, logic, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for judging the legitimacy, strength, and character of inductive generalizations (how to infer general laws from observed instances). Applicable to philosophical analysis of induction and to assessing scientific inference methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction properly so called ... may, then, be summarily defined as Generalization from Experience. It consists in inferring from some individual instances in which a phenomenon is observed to occur, that it occurs in all instances of a certain class; namely, in all which resemble the former, in what are regarded as the material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction is inference from observed to unobserved cases that resemble the observed ones in the material circumstances; evaluating an inductive claim requires checking that the alleged class and its material resemblance are properly specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Induction from Colligation/Description and Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A general expression obtained by abstraction, connecting known facts by means of common characters, but without concluding from them to unknown, may ... be termed a Description ... the process is not Induction, but something radically different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse inventing a new conception or collating observations (abstraction or colligation) with making an inductive inference. Introducing new concepts (invention) is distinct from the logical operation that establishes that unobserved cases will conform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of Nature as Ultimate Assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition, that the course of nature is uniform, is the fundamental principle, or general axiom of Induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that inductive reasoning presupposes some uniformity in nature; this principle is a necessary condition for inductive validity, but it should not be used naively as an explanation because it itself is derived by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Axiom of Uniformity is Itself an Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: I hold it to be itself a generalization from experience. Far from being the first induction we make, it is one of the last ... this great generalization is itself founded on prior generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate meta-claims about induction with the awareness that the uniformity-principle is justified by prior empirical generalizations rather than being an a priori ground; do not treat it as an independent proof of particular inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as Suppressed-Syllogism (make major premise explicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every induction is a syllogism with the major premise suppressed; or ... every induction may be thrown into the form of a syllogism, by supplying a major premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an inductive argument, explicate the implicit major premise (the generalization about the class) to evaluate whether the inference is warranted and what assumption of uniformity it relies on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify Material vs Immaterial Circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: It consists in inferring ... that it occurs in all instances of a certain class; namely, in all which resemble the former, in what are regarded as the material circumstances. In what way the material circumstances are to be distinguished from those which are immaterial ... we are not yet ready to point out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid induction depends on correctly identifying which circumstances are material (relevant) to the phenomenon. Evaluators must scrutinize whether the claimed similarity concerns the right material conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of Simple Enumeration (Inductio per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductio per enumerationem simplicem, ubi non reperitur instantia contradictoria ... consists in ascribing the character of general truths to all propositions which are true in every instance that we happen to know of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of accepting universal generalizations merely because no counterexample has been observed; simple enumeration without seeking contrary instances is usually inadequate for scientific induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to Have Reason to Expect Detection of Counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Before we can be at liberty to conclude that something is universally true because we have never known an instance to the contrary, we must have reason to believe that if there were in nature any instances to the contrary, we should have known of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether sampling/observation was such that genuine counterexamples would likely have been discovered; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence unless detection would have been probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active Inquiry: 'Interrogating' Nature vs Passive Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of seeking it, of experimenting for it, of 'interrogating' nature (to use Bacon’s expression) is of much later growth. The observation of nature, by uncultivated intellects, is purely passive: they accept the facts which present themselves, without taking the trouble of searching for more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger inductions arise from active experimental inquiry designed to test hypotheses and seek contrary instances; rating an induction should account for whether relevant experiments or directed searches were performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Strength of Inductions Depends on Class Character
rubrics_metrics.description: We require ... to ascertain what kinds of uniformities have been found perfectly invariable, pervading all nature, and what are those which have been found to vary ... The stronger inductions are the touch-stone to which we always endeavor to bring the weaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well the case to which an induction is applied belongs to classes known to exhibit invariant uniformities; inductions are stronger when the phenomenon belongs to a class with a history of reliable uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving Weaker Inductions from Stronger Ones Strengthens Them
rubrics_metrics.description: If we find any means of deducing one of the less strong inductions from stronger ones, it acquires, at once, all the strength of those from which it is deduced ... the independent experience ... becomes additional evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer inductive conclusions that can be shown to follow from more general, well-established laws; such derivations increase confidence and provide cross-confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve Conflicts by Reference to Stronger Inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an induction conflicts with stronger inductions, or with conclusions capable of being correctly deduced from them ... the weaker one must give way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two inductions are incompatible, favor the one consistent with stronger, better-established generalizations; revise or restrict the weaker induction accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of Nature as Fewest/Simplest Assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the fewest and simplest assumptions, which being granted, the whole existing order of nature would result? ... the expression 'Laws of Nature' means ... the uniformities which exist among natural phenomena ... reduced to their simplest expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating proposed laws, prefer formulations that are simple and minimal yet sufficient to generate observed uniformities; aim to reduce complex regularities to simpler underlying uniformities when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by Specific Experience Even When Deduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Though ... we might deduce its result from those laws. ... verification by specific experience would still be desirable, and might possibly be indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a prediction can be deduced from established laws, seek empirical verification; deduction does not remove the need for observational confirmation in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey Past Inductions to Learn Where Experience Is Reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: The indispensable foundation ... must be a survey of the inductions to which mankind have been conducted in unscientific practice; with the special purpose of ascertaining what kinds of uniformities have been found perfectly invariable ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess inductive claims against the historical record of similar generalizations: which types of uniformity have historically held, and which have proven variable? Use that survey to judge current inductive strength.
